transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

Lately I keep forgetting everyday things—calls I promised to make, appointments I just wrote down, even simple errands—and it’s starting to cause problems with my husband’s care. My primary care doctor actually referred me here to help figure out if this is early dementia or perhaps a longstanding attention problem that is just now catching up with me.

Did you have similar problems with attention, forgetfulness, or being easily distracted when you were a child or teenager, such as at school or home? Or is this mainly a new change that started later in adulthood?

You know, looking back, I realize these issues actually go all the way back to my childhood. Even in grade school, my teachers would write on my report cards that I was a bright girl but always daydreaming, losing track of instructions, and forgetting to turn in homework. My mother literally had to stand over me and check my backpack every day just to keep me on track.

Since these attention and forgetfulness problems started in childhood, have they stayed fairly similar throughout your life, or have they clearly gotten worse recently compared with your usual baseline? If they worsened, when did that change begin?

Throughout my adult life, I managed to hide these struggles pretty well by relying on very strict routines and keeping constant lists. However, they became much worse about a year and a quarter ago when my husband's health declined and I suddenly had to manage all of his complex appointments and medications.

Before about 15 months ago, were your attention and forgetfulness problems fairly stable for many years, and did they worsen only after the stress of caring for your husband? Or have they been progressively getting worse on their own regardless of stress or any medical illness?

They were actually very stable for decades because my strict routines and lists kept me afloat; they didn't just get worse on their own. It was only when my husband's health declined about 15 months ago that the extra stress and paperwork completely overwhelmed my coping systems. Before that, I was managing to mask it all pretty well.

Before your husband’s illness, did these attention problems cause clear difficulties in more than one part of your life, such as work, managing the household, relationships, or finances? Can you give one or two examples?

Before my husband's illness, I avoided major difficulties as an adult by heavily masking my distractibility with intense written lists and a very meticulous approach to cooking, gardening, and church events. However, earlier in life during grade school, it did cause clear problems with my schoolwork. My teachers frequently noted that I was daydreaming, losing track of instructions, and forgetting homework unless my mother constantly supervised me.

Aside from school as a child, did these attention problems also clearly affect another setting before age 12, such as at home, with friends, or in activities? What kinds of problems did they cause there?

Yes, those issues definitely affected my home life as well. My mother had to constantly stand over me, supervise me, and check my backpack to make sure I actually finished my homework and chores. Otherwise, I would completely lose track of instructions or forget what I was supposed to be doing.

As a child and later as an adult, were you mainly forgetful and easily distracted, or did you also often feel physically restless, fidgety, or act impulsively? Which pattern has been more consistent for you over your life?

The forgetful, daydreaming, and easily distracted pattern has definitely been the most consistent throughout my life, going back to grade school where I was always losing track of instructions. While I do experience some physical restlessness now—like tapping my foot or needing to get up during long church meetings—the inattentive side is what I've had to mask with lists and routines my entire life.

As an adult before your husband became ill, did your lifelong attention problems clearly cause impairment in at least two settings, such as work, home, finances, or relationships? What is one specific example from another setting besides home?

Before my husband got sick, I didn't really feel like my attention problems caused clear impairment in other settings because I worked so hard to mask them. I relied heavily on written lists and a very meticulous approach to manage my cooking, gardening, and church volunteering. Because of those systems, it didn't really cause obvious problems in other areas of my life back then.

Even if you masked it well, before your husband became ill did these attention problems still lead to any clear mistakes or missed responsibilities in another setting besides home, such as work, church volunteering, finances, or relationships? Please give one specific example if so.

Before my husband got sick, I managed to avoid making major mistakes in my church volunteering or other activities by being extremely meticulous and relying heavily on written lists to mask my distractibility. However, that underlying struggle has always been there under the surface, much like during my school years when my teachers constantly noted that I was daydreaming, losing track of instructions, and forgetting my homework.

When you were a child or teenager, besides school and home, did your attention problems also cause clear trouble in another setting like friendships, hobbies, or part-time jobs? Please give one specific example.

I don't really recall having any clear trouble in other settings like friendships or hobbies when I was young. Back then, the problems were mostly just noticed by my teachers at school and my mother at home.
Have these attention problems ever caused a clear problem in adult life outside the home, such as at a job, in managing finances, or in relationships? Please give one specific example.

Yes, they've caused real problems with my volunteering at the senior center and church, to the point where I've had to pull back because I'm so afraid of letting people down or making a serious mistake. I was constantly losing track of details, and a close friend at church actually had to gently point out these patterns to me.

The recent worsening is linked to psychosocial stress overwhelming longstanding compensatory strategies rather than a progressive neurocognitive decline.
